Grading Policies

Many of the policies in this course may differ significantly from what you expect from other classes, so please read this page carefully.

The design has three goals:

  1. Flexibility. You will get sick, have family obligations, oversleep, or simply have a bad week. The grading system accounts for all of that automatically, without you having to explain anything to anyone.
  2. Variety of evaluation. You will be evaluated in several different formats, so that no single format, and no single bad day, decides your grade.
  3. No need for individual exceptions. I am not in a position to judge whether a reason for missing class is a good one, and I do not want to be. I can only assess what you actually do. The rules are the same for everyone, and they are built so that you never need to ask for an exception.

These policies are designed to be challenging, but not difficult. The evaluations are serious: they ask you to show, in person and in real time, that you know the material and can reason with it. But the structure around them gives your final grade plenty of cushion, with generous engagement credit, more evaluation opportunities than you need, and only your best work counting.

The course also uses a partially flipped format, with some lecture material pre-recorded (see Course Format and Materials for how a typical class cycle works).

The Short Version

  • Do the readings and listen to or watch the recorded lectures before class, and bring the right materials (see Course Format and Materials). Nearly everything graded happens in class and depends on that preparation.
  • Your grade has two categories, each worth 50%: evaluation and engagement.
  • If you prepare for class and come to most sessions, you do not need to worry about the mechanics on this page. The system takes care of you.
  • If you are having a rough semester, you will still have plenty of opportunities to do well, without requesting absences, extensions, or exceptions.
  • Please do not email me about absences or missed work. You do not need to, and doing so will cost you points (see Reading These Guidelines, below).

Evaluation (50%)

Evaluation measures how well you have mastered the course material: both what you know and how well you reason with it (see Learning Outcomes).

How It Works

  • All evaluation assignments take place in class, many of them by hand. (Why? See AI in This Course.)
  • They are not announced in advance. Come prepared every time. (Do not stress, though: there are many opportunities, such that the stakes for any single evaluation are low.)
  • Anything assigned up to that day is fair game: recorded lectures, readings, primary sources, and live lecture.
  • Formats vary: handwritten mini-essays, short-response questions, moderated discussions, and presentations. For written work, see also the Writing Guidelines.
  • Only your best two evaluation grades count. All others are dropped.

Because only your best two grades count, a missed evaluation requires no action from you. If you are absent on an evaluation day, or you are present but would rather not complete that day’s evaluation, that is your call. There is nothing to report and nothing to make up.

Rotations

Every student is assigned to one of eight rotations, labeled “blue,” “green,” etc. A rotation is not a group project or a team. It is simply a scheduling device that determines who is evaluated on which day. Not all sorts of evaluations can feasibly involve the entire class: the purpose of this system is to equitably stagger them throughout the semester.

You are always evaluated and graded individually, and your grade never depends on anyone else’s work.

On a given day, I might evaluate the whole class, a single rotation, two rotations, or half the class. Students who are not being evaluated that day work on something else, which counts toward engagement.

Rotations are called in a strict cycle, so every rotation receives the same number of opportunities. If you come to most classes, you will have many more chances to complete an evaluation than the two that count. Each additional evaluation is a chance to replace a weaker grade with a better one, so you can miss several and still be in good shape.

Rotation assignments are final. There is no switching rotations for any reason, and rotations are not rebalanced if students drop the course.

Rules

  • No make-ups, early, or late evaluations. Ever. Rest assured that if you miss an evaluation you will soon have another opportunity (with only the highest two grades counting when the dust settles).
  • Scanned submissions: many evaluations are handwritten, scanned, and uploaded to Canvas (see What to Bring in Course Format and Materials).
  • Late arrival: if you arrive after an evaluation has begun, you cannot take part in it. No exceptions.
  • Grading: every evaluation is graded against clear criteria, which I will explain in class. Grades are not open to negotiation. If you are unhappy with a grade, the best remedy is to come to class: your next evaluation will probably replace it.
  • A benefit of regular attendance: students who come to class consistently will have more opportunities than they need, so in practice they can let their two best formats count. Students who miss many sessions lose that leeway, regardless of the reason for the absence (except in unusual circumstances: see below).
  • Fewer than two grades: if you end the semester with fewer than two evaluation grades, each missing grade counts as a zero. This happens only if you miss a very large share of the semester (see Do Absences Ever Matter?, below).

Engagement (50%)

Engagement is a participation category with a finish line. Reach 100 points and you have full credit (100%). Many more than 100 points will be available over the semester, roughly twice as many, so you can miss a substantial number of sessions or activities and still reach 100. If you come to class regularly, you will reach 100% well before the end of the semester, which means this entire grade category is likely to serve as a cushion offsetting the evaluation category.

Ways to Earn Engagement Points

  • In-class quizzes based on the recorded lectures (see Course Format and Materials).
  • In-class activities and exercises, including the activities that run while other rotations are being evaluated.
  • Contributions to live discussion, in-class polls, and the in-class question forum.
  • Notes checks: occasionally I will ask to see your notes in class (see Note-Taking).
  • Office hours visits to discuss course content (a limited number of visits count).

Rules

  • Points cannot be earned after the fact. A quiz that has closed stays closed; an activity that has passed is gone. There will be many others.
  • Engagement points stop accruing at the last class meeting.
  • On days when your rotation is being evaluated, you will not do that day’s engagement activity. Because every rotation is called equally often, this evens out for everyone.

Going Past the Finish Line

For every 10 engagement points beyond 100, I add 1 point to your evaluation score, up to a maximum of 10 points. If you engage thoroughly all semester, hard work can raise your evaluation score.

This is the only extra credit in the course. Please do not ask about other extra credit.

Example: Jeff’s semester

Jeff Winger is a busy guy. He works about twenty hours a week at a law office, loses a week in October to the flu, and is, by his own account, “pacing himself.” He misses roughly a third of class sessions, including one for reasons he describes only as “a Greendale thing.” He never emails me about any of it, so he keeps his 10 guidelines points.

Evaluation. Jeff is in the green rotation (go Human Beings). Between absences, and one day when he decides to sit an evaluation out, he completes four evaluations, scoring 64, 71, 58, and 77. Only his best two count: (77 + 71) ÷ 2 = 74.

Engagement. By mid-November, Jeff has 104 engagement points (including his 10 guidelines points), which is already full credit. Then, sensing an opportunity, he spends the last few weeks doing everything on offer and finishes with 127.

Going past the finish line. 127 is 27 points past 100. Each full 10 points adds 1 point to evaluation, so Jeff earns 2 bonus points (the leftover 7 don’t count). His evaluation score rises from 74 to 76.

Final grade: (50% × 76) + (50% × 100) = 88.

Jeff missed a third of the semester, skipped an evaluation on purpose, and never explained himself to anyone. None of that required an exception. His grade reflects the work he actually did, including the extra push at the end.

Reading These Guidelines: 10 Points

Every student automatically receives 10 engagement points for reading and understanding these guidelines.

You keep them as long as you do not email me about absences, missed work, extensions, exceptions, make-ups, regrades, extra credit, or rotation changes. If you send such an email, you forfeit these points.

None of this applies when there is something fundamentally more serious to discuss: a disability accommodation through Disability Resources and Services (DRS), or circumstances serious enough to affect your semester as a whole (see Unusual Circumstances, below). And questions about course content, or about arranging an office hours meeting, are always welcome.

If something on this page is unclear, ask in class or in office hours.

Does This Mean I Don’t Want to Hear from You?

Absolutely not. Quite the contrary, in fact. I want to talk with you about the ideas, sources, and arguments of this course; I just don’t want our conversations to be about absences and exceptions. Visits to office hours to discuss course content also earn engagement points (see Ways to Earn Engagement Points, above).

Email

Email is always welcome for questions about course content, ideas, and readings; for arranging office hours; and for passing along an opportunity the whole class might enjoy, such as a lecture, an event, or an exhibit.

Emails about absences, missed work, extensions, exceptions, make-ups, regrades, extra credit, or rotation changes aren’t necessary: the rules on this page already handle all of them. I will still read and answer them, but sending one costs the 10 guidelines points (see above). Think of it as a small fee for a service you don’t need.

When you do email, see Email Etiquette.

Do Absences Ever Matter?

Missing a few classes, or even quite a few, requires no action from you. Even ending the semester with only three evaluation grades would be nothing to worry about, since only two count. To be in real danger of falling below two, you would have to miss something like half the semester.

If you find yourself there, then yes, please get in touch with me. But the conversation will not be about individual absences: it will be about Unusual Circumstances (below). Contacting me in that situation never costs you the 10 guidelines points.

Unusual Circumstances

The rules on this page are built to absorb ordinary disruptions. Some situations go beyond that. Communication about any of the following never affects the 10 guidelines points.

Disability Accommodations

If you have accommodations through Disability Resources and Services (DRS), follow the DRS process for sharing your accommodation letter. Depending on your accommodations, your arrangements may differ substantially from those described on this page. The course’s Alternative Grading Option is likely to apply, though no single arrangement can anticipate every need.

Serious Disruptions

If something serious, such as an extended illness or a family emergency, keeps you away from a large part of the semester, get in touch with me. Also contact your academic advisor or the Dean of Students office, who coordinate with instructors in these situations and through whom the Alternative Grading Option is arranged. That option is likely to apply; other arrangements under university policy (for example, an incomplete or a withdrawal) are also possible.

How Your Final Grade Is Calculated

  • Evaluation score = the average of your best two evaluation grades, plus any engagement bonus (maximum 100).
  • Engagement score = your engagement points, up to 100.
  • Final grade = 50% evaluation + 50% engagement.

Letter grades follow Canvas’s standard cutoffs, with no rounding up or down: your final percentage determines your letter grade.

Official category totals are posted in Canvas periodically throughout the semester.

Frequently Asked Questions

I missed class. What should I do?
Watch any recorded lectures you missed, compare notes with colleagues, and come to the next class prepared. You should not inform the instructor: the system already has you covered.

My rotation was called on a day I was absent. Is that fair?
Every rotation receives the same number of opportunities, and only your best two grades count.

Is this group work?
No. Rotations only determine scheduling. Some evaluations, such as moderated discussions, involve talking with other students, but you are always graded individually.

What if you can’t read my handwriting?
Unlikely: I decipher historical handwriting for a living. But not to worry. If I can’t make out your handwriting, I will invite you to office hours to read it out loud for me.

Can I switch rotations?
No.

Can I make up a quiz or an in-class activity?
No. Many more are available than you need.

I’m unhappy with an evaluation grade. Can we discuss it?
I’m glad to talk in office hours about how to do better next time. The grade itself stands, and if you keep coming to class, it will probably be dropped.

Is there extra credit?
Only the engagement bonus described above.

I’m having a really hard semester. What are my options?
If you are missing a few classes here and there, the system already accounts for it. If you are missing a large part of the semester, see Unusual Circumstances.
